title: Numeral systems (decimal, binary, hexadecimal, and octal)
recap: C++ binary literals use a 0b prefix and hexadecimal literals use 0x. Apostrophes can separate digits for readability without changing a literal's value.
std::bitset provides fixed-width binary output. Stream base manipulators such as std::hex are sticky, so later integer output remains hexadecimal until std::dec resets the stream.
objectives: Represent an eight-bit value with a grouped binary literal.
Represent a nibble mask with a hexadecimal literal.
Reset a sticky hexadecimal stream state before decimal output.
warnings: std::cout has no std::bin manipulator; use std::bitset for binary output.
std::hex affects subsequent integral insertions until another base manipulator is applied.
The binary, hexadecimal, and decimal spellings in this exercise represent values, not strings to print directly.
challenge: Write status as the grouped binary literal 0b1010'1100 and lowNibbleMask as the unsigned hexadecimal literal 0x0Fu. Keep std::bitset<8> for the binary display, then explicitly reset the sticky std::hex formatting with std::dec so status is finally shown as decimal 172.
hints: Change the status initializer to a 0b-prefixed literal and group its two nibbles with an apostrophe.
The unsigned hexadecimal spelling of decimal 15 is 0x0Fu; std::hex controls how its value is displayed.
Insert std::dec into the stream before status on the final line because std::hex remains active.
